title: Accessible name contradicts the visible button label
description: The Delete observation button carries aria-label="Save observation". A mouse user reads Delete; an assistive-technology user hears Save. A non-empty accessible name therefore passes the automated name checks while describing the wrong action.

relatedElements.note: Identical button whose accessible name matches the visible label.

expectedBehaviour: The accessible name of a control contains the visible label text, so that the name and the visible action agree.
actualBehaviour: The visible label is Delete observation, but aria-label replaces the accessible name with Save observation.
userImpact: Voice-control users cannot activate the button by speaking its visible label, and screen-reader users are told the button does something other than what it does.

wcag.note: The accessible name does not contain the visible label text.
The name is available to assistive technology but describes a different action.

observed.note: Page-level axe run with tags wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa and best-practice. The rule reports the visible Delete observation label against the Save observation accessible name.

detection.note: Automated name checks pass because the name is non-empty. Comparing the name with the visible label needs a human review or a heuristic check.

manualTests: Open the accessibility tree for both buttons and compare each accessible name with the text printed on the button.
Try to activate variant A by voice using its visible label.

assistiveTechnologyTests.procedure: Navigate to the target with the VoiceOver rotor and confirm what is announced.

assertions: Variant A exposes the accessible name Save observation while displaying Delete observation.
tests: tests/subtle-defects.spec.js: keeps the misleading accessible name on variant A

reviewStatus.note: A Playwright regression test preserves the defective behaviour and its control. That is automated reproduction, not a manual or assistive-technology observation.
